overview: The SAVES Act would create a Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) pilot program that gives competitive grants of up to $2 million each to nonprofit groups that train and provide service dogs to veterans. To qualify, a veteran must be enrolled in VA health care, have a service dog prescribed by the VA, and have a condition such as blindness, hearing loss, loss of a limb or paralysis, post-traumatic stress disorder, or traumatic brain injury. The nonprofits could not charge veterans for the dogs, would have to train both the dogs and the veterans, and would have to follow humane treatment standards; the VA could also buy veterinary insurance for the dogs. The bill authorizes $10 million a year from 2027 through 2031, and the program would end on September 30, 2031. It also extends to February 2033 an existing limit on certain VA pension payments. As of September 26, 2025, the House Veterans' Affairs Committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar.
for: Supporters say trained service dogs can help veterans with disabilities and conditions like PTSD live more independently, and funding experienced nonprofits would get more dogs to veterans at no cost to them.
against: Critics say the VA could fund an expanded program before the evidence on service dogs for conditions like PTSD is fully settled, and that grants to outside groups require close oversight to make sure the money is well spent.
